docs.title: statlite
docs.text:
A small, dependency-free statistics library, and the demo project for the Advanced GitHub workshop.

import statlite

statlite.mean([1, 2, 3, 4])  # 2.5
statlite.percentile([1, 2, 3, 4], 25)  # 1.75
statlite.pearson([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6])  # 1.0

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Descriptive statistics: mean, median, mode, variance, stdev
  • Quantiles: percentile, iqr
  • Association: covariance, pearson
  • Fully typed, documented with NumPy-style docstrings, no runtime dependencies

Note

These docs are rebuilt on every merge to main (the dev version) and versioned for every tagged release.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Pick or open an issue.
  2. Create a branch from an up-to-date main: git switch -c feature/<short-name>.
  3. Make small, focused commits with clear messages.
  4. Run the checks locally (see below), then push and open a pull request.
  5. Address review comments. When CI is green and you have an approval, the PR is merged into main.

docs.title: Local checks
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pre-commit install

ruff format --check .
ruff check .
mypy
pytest
mkdocs build --strict

docs.title: Code standards
docs.text:
• Format and lint with ruff; all public functions need NumPy-style docstrings with an Examples section (doctests are run in CI).
  • Type annotations are required and checked with mypy --strict.
  • New behavior needs tests; coverage must stay at or above 90%.
  • Add a line to CHANGELOG.md under Unreleased.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
Releases are tag-driven. The version is derived from the git tag, so there is no version number to edit.

git tag -a v0.2.0 -m "v0.2.0"
git push origin v0.2.0

docs.title: Install
docs.text: pip install -i https://test.pypi.org/simple/ statlite

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from statlite import mean, stdev, pearson

heights = [1.62, 1.75, 1.80, 1.68, 1.71]
weights = [58, 72, 80, 63, 68]

print(mean(heights))
print(stdev(heights))  # sample standard deviation (ddof=1)
print(pearson(heights, weights))

Every function accepts any iterable of numbers and raises ValueError for invalid input, such as empty data.

docs.title: statlite.correlation
docs.text: Measures of association between two variables.

docs.title: covariance(x, y, ddof=1)
docs.text:
Compute the covariance of two equal-length samples.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x Iterable of float

The paired samples. Must have the same length, greater than ddof.

required y Iterable of float

The paired samples. Must have the same length, greater than ddof.

required ddof int

Delta degrees of freedom. Use 1 for the sample covariance.

1

Returns:

Type Description float

The covariance.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the samples differ in length or are too short.

Examples:

>>> covariance([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6])
2.0

docs.title: pearson(x, y)
docs.text:
Compute the Pearson correlation coefficient.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x Iterable of float

The paired samples. Must have the same length, at least 2.

required y Iterable of float

The paired samples. Must have the same length, at least 2.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The correlation, between -1 and 1.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the samples differ in length, are too short, or either has zero variance.

Examples:

>>> pearson([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6])
1.0

docs.title: statlite.descriptive
docs.text: Descriptive statistics: measures of center and spread.

docs.title: mean(data)
docs.text:
Compute the arithmetic mean.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Iterable of float

The input values. Must contain at least one value.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The arithmetic mean.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If data is empty.

Examples:

>>> mean([1, 2, 3, 4])
2.5

docs.title: median(data)
docs.text:
Compute the median.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Iterable of float

The input values. Must contain at least one value.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The middle value, or the mean of the two middle values.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If data is empty.

Examples:

>>> median([3, 1, 2])
2.0
>>> median([4, 1, 3, 2])
2.5

docs.title: mode(data)
docs.text:
Compute the most common value.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Iterable of float

The input values. Must contain at least one value.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The most frequent value. Ties are broken by the smallest value.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If data is empty.

Examples:

>>> mode([1, 2, 2, 3])
2.0
>>> mode([1, 1, 2, 2])
1.0

docs.title: stdev(data, ddof=1)
docs.text:
Compute the standard deviation.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Iterable of float

The input values. Must contain more than ddof values.

required ddof int

Delta degrees of freedom. See :func:variance.

1

Returns:

Type Description float

The standard deviation, the square root of :func:variance.

Examples:

>>> stdev([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9], ddof=0)
2.0

docs.title: variance(data, ddof=1)
docs.text:
Compute the variance.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Iterable of float

The input values. Must contain more than ddof values.

required ddof int

Delta degrees of freedom. Use 1 for the sample variance and 0 for the population variance.

1

Returns:

Type Description float

The variance.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If there are not more than ddof values, or ddof is negative.

Examples:

>>> variance([1, 2, 3, 4])
1.6666666666666667
>>> variance([1, 2, 3, 4], ddof=0)
1.25

docs.title: iqr(data)
docs.text:
Compute the interquartile range (75th minus 25th percentile).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Iterable of float

The input values. Must contain at least one value.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The interquartile range.

Examples:

>>> iqr([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
2.0

docs.title: percentile(data, q)
docs.text:
Compute the q-th percentile using linear interpolation.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Iterable of float

The input values. Must contain at least one value.

required q float

The percentile to compute, between 0 and 100 inclusive.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The interpolated percentile.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If data is empty or q is outside [0, 100].

Examples:

>>> percentile([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 50)
3.0
>>> percentile([1, 2, 3, 4], 25)
1.75
